extracted.intended_audience: political philosophers, legislators, statesmen, and students of constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for designing, judging, and maintaining city-states and their institutions (magistracies, property rules, public provisions, definitions of citizenship) drawn from Aristotle's discussion of Lacedaemon, Crete, Carthage, and other constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of property
rubrics_metrics.description: Fault may be found with his unequal division of property, for some will have far too much, others too little; by which means the land will come into few hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that unequal land distribution concentrates property, reduces the able-bodied citizen-population (e.g., inability to field sufficient soldiers), and increases poverty and avarice. He criticizes rules that prohibit buying/selling but allow bequests, since similar consequences (concentration of wealth) follow. He even notes that large inheritances through women can concentrate nearly two parts in five of the country in female hands, recommending regulation of inheritance to prevent imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population policy must align with property distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The law to encourage population (e.g., exemptions for men with three or four children) was by no means calculated to correct this inequality; though intended to make Spartans numerous, while land remained divided, many would be very poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that reward larger families (tax exemptions, exemptions from duties) can backfire if land/resource distribution does not permit sustainable subsistence for an increased population. Population incentives must be designed with land/economic structures in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and eligibility of magistrates (ephori/kosmoi)
rubrics_metrics.description: These magistrates take cognisance of things of the last importance, and yet they are chosen out of the people in general; so that it often happens that a very poor person is elected to that office, who, from that circumstance, is easily bought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electing important magistrates indiscriminately risks bribery and corruption. Magistrates who wield great power should be chosen by a method that secures probity and competence (Aristotle contrasts Lacedaemonian ephori with the Carthaginian hundred-and-four chosen 'out of those of the better sort'). The mode of election matters: selection should avoid easily corruptible socioeconomic profiles and should be structured to preserve the state's parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power distribution and checks (avoid near-tyrannical magistracies)
rubrics_metrics.description: These men, being corrupted with money, went as far as they could to ruin the city: and, because their power was too great and nearly tyrannical, their kings were obliged to flatter them, which contributed greatly to hurt the state; so that it altered from an aristocracy to a democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magistracies that concentrate excessive power without proper checks can destabilize constitutions, force other offices into subservience, and provoke constitutional degeneration. Effective checks and balance mechanisms are required to prevent oligarchic or tyrannical concentration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-making according to written law or established custom
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not right that they should determine according to their own opinion, but by a written law or established custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For magistrates dealing with matters 'of the last consequence' (supreme judges), decisions should be governed by written law or established customs rather than accidental individual discretion; reliance on arbitrary decision-making undermines stability and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure and accountability of senators
rubrics_metrics.description: But still it might be debated whether they should be continued judges for life, to determine points of the greatest moment, since the mind has its old age as well as the body; ... they have been guilty both of bribery and partiality in many public affairs; for which reason it had been much better if they had been made answerable for their conduct, which they are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Life tenure without accountability risks deterioration of judgment and corruption. Senators/judges exercising high functions should face mechanisms for accountability or limited tenure to maintain competence and prevent bribery/partiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusivity of public provisions (public meals/common tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their common meals at first were not well established: these should rather have been provided at the public expense ... for he intended that those public meals should strengthen the democratic part of his government: but this regulation had quite the contrary effect, for those who were very poor could not take part in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If public institutions meant to foster civic unity (e.g., common meals) require private contributions, the poor will be excluded and the intended democratic strengthening fails. Community-provided provisioning (as at Crete) better secures participation across classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid constitutions designed solely for war
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato has given ... that the whole constitution was calculated only for the business of war: it is indeed excellent to make them conquerors; for which reason the preservation of the state depended thereon. The destruction of it commenced with their victories: for they knew not how to be idle, or engage in any other employment than war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutions that organize society solely around military aims produce societies unable to pursue peaceful occupations or civic prosperity; victory can exacerbate degeneration by preventing adaptation to peacetime needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective public revenue and subsidy systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor was the public revenue well managed at Sparta, for the state was worth nothing while they were obliged to carry on the most extensive wars, and the subsidies were very badly raised; for as the Spartans possessed a large extent of country, they were not exact upon each other as to what they paid in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poorly administered taxation and subsidy systems leave the state impoverished and individuals avaricious. The legislator must ensure accurate, enforceable revenue collection to maintain state capacity and public goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selecting magistrates solely by wealth (prevent oligarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible for those who are in bad circumstances to support the dignity of their office ... as choosing men of fortune to be magistrates make a state incline to an oligarchy, and men of abilities to an aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a trade-off: selecting wealthy magistrates secures leisure but risks oligarchy and venality; selecting by ability supports aristocracy of merit. The legislator should guard against degeneration by ensuring capable citizens can serve without being excluded for poverty (e.g., provide sufficient leisure/support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent venality by ensuring leisure for men of merit
rubrics_metrics.description: It would have been better for the legislature to have passed over the poverty of men of merit, and only to have taken care to have ensured them sufficient leisure, when in office, to attend to public affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States should secure that meritorious but poor citizens have material conditions (time, resources) to serve, rather than forcing selection toward the wealthy who can afford office, which encourages purchase of offices and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization and non-accumulation of offices
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems also improper, that one person should execute several offices ... one business is best done by one person; and it is the duty of the legislator to look to this, and not make the same person a musician and a shoemaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid concentrating multiple unrelated public functions in one individual; division of labor increases efficiency and reduces opportunities for abuse of combined powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional remedies should be lawful and stable (not ad hoc resignations or turn-outs)
rubrics_metrics.description: They are also permitted to resign their office before their time is elapsed, and if all this was done by law it would be well, and not at the pleasure of the individuals, which is a bad rule to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resignation or removal of magistrates must follow established legal procedures; ad hoc or discretionary practices create instability and enable factional manipulation (e.g., conspiracies to turn out magistrates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional design must minimise room for insurrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas the legislator ought to frame his government, that there be no room for insurrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-designed constitution should embed mechanisms preventing the structural causes of revolt (e.g., exclusion, concentration of wealth/power). Relying on chance or ad hoc accommodations with popular parties is insufficient to guarantee stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a full citizen by participation in government
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing that more characterises a complete citizen than having a share in the judicial and executive part of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle defines a full citizen not by residence or mere legal privileges but by the right to partake in public offices (judicial/executive). Partial participants (sojourners, slaves, unenrolled youths, aged past service) are not complete citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizenship criteria: ancestry, legal creation, and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: In common use they define a citizen to be one who is sprung from citizens on both sides ... but some persons have questioned how the first of the family could prove themselves citizens ... As Philolaus gave them laws concerning many other things, so did he upon adoption ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle records debates over ancestry-based definitions (both parents), ancestral depth, and the status of citizens created by revolution or grant. He notes problems with rigid ancestry rules for first founders and admits that legally created (even illegally created) citizens may continue to function as citizens though the justice of their creation is a separate question.

rubrics_metrics.name: The city's identity depends on its constitution (governmental form)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we speak of a city as being the same we refer to the government there established; and this, whether it is called by the same name or any other, or inhabited by the same men or different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in the species of government (e.g., aristocracy→democracy→tyranny) may render a polity 'different' even if place and people remain. Political identity is tied to the constitution, so evaluating continuity should focus on form of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of judicial and executive functions defines citizenship and government type
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial also of different causes is allotted to different persons ... some being to be heard by one magistrate, others by another ... at Lacedaemon all disputes concerning contracts are brought before some of the ephori: the senate are the judges in cases of murder ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which institutions hear which causes (who judges contracts vs murders, etc.) is a constitutive feature of government type and affects who counts as a citizen (who is eligible to perform these functions). Evaluation of constitutions must attend to institutional jurisdictional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid centralising all causes in same magistrates without safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: The determining all causes by the same magistrates, and not orae in one court and another in another, as at Lacedaemon, has the same influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizing jurisdiction in a small body can incline a state toward oligarchy; distribution of judicial forums can be a check on concentrated power and preserve mixed constitution balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of selection (suffrage vs lot) and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: As they are not elected by lot, but by suffrage, and are not permitted to take money, they are the greatest supporters imaginable of an aristocracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection method has normative consequences: election by suffrage tends to privilege ability or wealth and can support aristocracy; selection by lot distributes eligibility more widely. Rules about bribery/compensation also affect the character of the office and of the regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of magistracy by family/clan vs whole community
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the Cretans the kosmoi are not chosen out of the people in general, but out of some certain families, and the senate out of the kosmoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricting eligibility to certain families creates oligarchic tendencies and undermines broader civic investment. Inclusive eligibility strengthens popular attachment to the state, while family-based selection risks dynastic or aristocratic capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing factional violence and lawless force
rubrics_metrics.description: What is worst of all is, that general confusion which those who are in power introduce to impede the ordinary course of justice ... it is usual with the principal persons amongst them to collect together some of the common people and their friends, and then revolt and set up for themselves, and come to blows with each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal frameworks must prevent and penalize the use of factional mobs and private force to alter governance; toleration of such practices dissolves constitutional order either quickly (insurrection) or gradually (constitutional decay).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator's aim: avoid making citizens completely virtuous but secure institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: But that the legislator himself did not expect to make all his citizens honourable and completely virtuous is evident ... he distrusts them as not being good men; for he sent those upon the same embassy that were at variance with each other; and thought, that in the dispute of the kings the safety of the state consisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should not rely on perfect virtue in citizens; institutions should assume human fallibility and create structures (dividing power, checks) that harness self-interest to the state's safety (e.g., putting rivals together so their dispute secures balance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding political effects of social customs (e.g., sexual practices) without consideration of broader consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: He also endeavoured, that his community might not be too populous, to lessen the connection with women, by introducing the love of boys: whether in this he did well or ill we shall have some other opportunity of considering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislator's attempts to influence social/customary practices (marriage, sexual norms) for demographic or civic ends carry broader moral and political consequences and must be judged in context; social engineering can have unintended effects on family structure and civic stability.
